questions.question:
The relationship between oxygen consumption and equivalent biodegradable organic
removal (i.e. BOD) in a closed container with respect to time is shown in the figure. Assume that the rate of oxygen consumption is directly proportional to the amount of
degradable organic matter and is expressed as [latex]\frac{dL_t}{dt}=-kL_t[/latex], where, [latex]L_t[/latex] (in mg/litre) is the oxygen equivalent of the organics remaining at time t and [latex]k[/latex] (in [latex]d^{-1}[/latex]) is the degradation
rate constant. [latex]L_0[/latex] is the oxygen of organic matter at time, t = 0. In the above context, the correct expression is
questions.explanation:
Given, [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dL_t}{dt}&=-kL_t \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{dL_t}{L_t} &=-kdt \\ \Rightarrow \; \int_{L_o}^{L_t} \frac{dL_t}{L_t} &=-k\int_{0}^{t}dt \\ \Rightarrow \; \ln \left ( \frac{L_t}{L_o} \right ) &=-kt \\ \Rightarrow \; L_t&=L_o e^{-kt} \end{aligned}[/latex] The term [latex]L_o[/latex] in the above equation represents
the total oxygen equivalent of the organics at
time [latex]t=0[/latex], while [latex]L_t[/latex] represents the amount
remaining at time [latex]t[/latex], and decays exponentially
with time. The amount of oxygen used in the consumption
of the organics, the [latex]{BOD}_t[/latex]
 can be found from the [latex]L_t[/latex] value. The difference between the value [latex]L_o[/latex] and [latex]L_t[/latex] is
the oxygen equivalent consumed, or the BOD
exerted. Mathematically [latex]{BOD}_t=(L_o-L_t)=L_o-L_oe^{-kt}=L_o(1-e^{-kt})[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dL_t}{dt}&=-kL_t \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{dL_t}{L_t} &=-kdt \\ \Rightarrow \; \int_{L_o}^{L_t} \frac{dL_t}{L_t} &=-k\int_{0}^{t}dt \\ \Rightarrow \; \ln \left ( \frac{L_t}{L_o} \right ) &=-kt \\ \Rightarrow \; L_t&=L_o e^{-kt} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The term [latex]L_o[/latex] in the above equation represents the total oxygen equivalent of the organics at time [latex]t=0[/latex], while [latex]L_t[/latex] represents the amount remaining at time [latex]t[/latex], and decays exponentially with time.
The amount of oxygen used in the consumption of the organics, the [latex]{BOD}_t[/latex] can be found from the [latex]L_t[/latex] value.
The difference between the value [latex]L_o[/latex] and [latex]L_t[/latex] is the oxygen equivalent consumed, or the BOD exerted. Mathematically
[latex]{BOD}_t=(L_o-L_t)=L_o-L_oe^{-kt}=L_o(1-e^{-kt})[/latex]

for removal of these particles is

options.A: settling chamber followed by bag filter
options.B: electrostatic precipitator followed by venturi scrubber
options.C: electrostatic precipitator followed by cyclonic separator
options.D: bag filter followed by electrostatic precipitator

questions.explanation:
Large size particles should be removed first, hence answer should be (A). Theoretically, gravitational settling chamber
should be able to remove particulates down to 5
or 10 [latex]\mu m[/latex], but in actual they are not practical for
removal of particles much less than 50 [latex]\mu m[/latex] in
size. Hence, gravitational settling chamber is most
suitable choice for removal of suspended particles
of size 50 [latex]\mu m[/latex]. After the removal of 50 [latex]\mu m[/latex] size particles, to
remove 2 [latex]\mu m[/latex] size particles, we use fabric bag
filter. Note: Fabric bag filter has high collection
efficiency for all particle sizes, especially for
particles smaller than 10 [latex]\mu m[/latex] in diameter.
questions.explanation_html:
Large size particles should be removed first, hence answer should be (A).
Theoretically, gravitational settling chamber should be able to remove particulates down to 5 or 10 [latex]\mu m[/latex], but in actual they are not practical for removal of particles much less than 50 [latex]\mu m[/latex] in size.
Hence, gravitational settling chamber is most suitable choice for removal of suspended particles of size 50 [latex]\mu m[/latex].
After the removal of 50 [latex]\mu m[/latex] size particles, to remove 2 [latex]\mu m[/latex] size particles, we use fabric bag filter.

A waste to energy plant burns dry solid waste of composition : Carbon = 35%, Oxygen = 26%, Hydrogen = 10%, Sulphur = 6%, Nitrogen = 3% and Inerts = 20%. Burning rate is 1000 tonnes/d. Oxygen in air by weight is 23%. Assume complete
conversion of Carbon to [latex]CO_2[/latex], Hydrogen to [latex]H_2O[/latex], Sulphur to [latex]SO_2[/latex] and Nitrogen to [latex]NO_2[/latex]. Given Atomic weighs : H=1, C=12, N=14, O=16, S=32. The stoichiometric (theoretical) amount of air (in tonnes/d, round off to the nearest integer)
required for complete burning of this waste, is __________.
questions.explanation: [latex]\underbrace{C}_{12}\underbrace{O}_{2}\rightarrow CO_2[/latex] Oxygen required for 350 tonne/day [latex]\frac{32}{12}\times 350=933.33[/latex] [latex]\underbrace{4H}_{4}+\underbrace{O_2}_{32}\rightarrow 2H_2O[/latex] Oxygen required for 100 tonne/day [latex]\frac{32}{4}\times 100=800[/latex] [latex]\underbrace{S}_{32}+\underbrace{O_2}_{32}\rightarrow SO_2[/latex] Oxygen required for 60 tonne/day [latex]\frac{32}{32}\times 60=60[/latex] [latex]\underbrace{N}_{14}+\underbrace{O}_{32}\rightarrow NO_2[/latex] Oxygen required for 30 tonne/day [latex]\frac{32}{14}\times 30=68.57[/latex] Total [latex]O_2[/latex] = 1861.9 tonne/day Available [latex]O_2[/latex] in waste = 260 tonne/day Required =1861.9-260=1601.9 tinne/day Amount of air required [latex]=\frac{1601.9}{0.23}=6964.78 \; \text{tonne/day} \simeq 6965 \; \text{tonne/day}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\underbrace{C}_{12}\underbrace{O}_{2}\rightarrow CO_2[/latex]
Oxygen required for 350 tonne/day
[latex]\frac{32}{12}\times 350=933.33[/latex]
[latex]\underbrace{4H}_{4}+\underbrace{O_2}_{32}\rightarrow 2H_2O[/latex]
Oxygen required for 100 tonne/day
[latex]\frac{32}{4}\times 100=800[/latex]
[latex]\underbrace{S}_{32}+\underbrace{O_2}_{32}\rightarrow SO_2[/latex]
Oxygen required for 60 tonne/day
[latex]\frac{32}{32}\times 60=60[/latex]
[latex]\underbrace{N}_{14}+\underbrace{O}_{32}\rightarrow NO_2[/latex]
Oxygen required for 30 tonne/day
[latex]\frac{32}{14}\times 30=68.57[/latex]
Total [latex]O_2[/latex] = 1861.9 tonne/day
Available [latex]O_2[/latex] in waste = 260 tonne/day
Required =1861.9-260=1601.9 tinne/day
Amount of air required [latex]=\frac{1601.9}{0.23}=6964.78 \; \text{tonne/day} \simeq 6965 \; \text{tonne/day}[/latex]
